messages.subject_clean: Aroma took me a long time for processing Affy 6.0 data
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

    We are using Aroma to preprocess Cel files for GWA studies. I ran
the following steps. The algorithm works very well except the last
step, which is very very slow. For one plate (about 90 Cel files), the
first two steps can be finished in about half a day. But the last step
has not finished yet after four days running.

    Is this expected?

Thanks.

Jerry

Here is the code:

    cdf <- AffymetrixCdfFile$fromChipType("GenomeWideSNP_6",
tags="Full")
    gi <- getGenomeInformation(cdf)
    si <- getSnpInformation(cdf)
    cs <- AffymetrixCelSet$fromName(plate, cdf=cdf)
    acc <- AllelicCrosstalkCalibration(cs)
    csC <- process(acc, verbose=verbose)
    plm <- AvgCnPlm(csC, mergeStrands=TRUE, combineAlleles=TRUE, shift=
+300)
    ces <- getChipEffectSet(plm)
    fln <- FragmentLengthNormalization(ces)
    cesN <- process(fln, verbose=verbose)

messages.subject: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] Re: memory problem - extractRawCopyNumbers
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

extractRawCopyNumbers(cbs) caches the results *in memory* in the 'cbs'
object.  This is why you run out of memory.  By calling gc(cbs), you
will clear the cache of the 'cbs' object.  I suggest you do this
immediately after and each time you are calling
extractRawCopyNumbers(), e.g.

rawCNs <- extractRawCopyNumbers(cbs, array=j, chromosome=k)$cn;
gc(cbs);

FYI, the extractRawCopyNumbers() was added as an ad hoc solution in
the beginning, which is probably why the results are cached by
default.  In the next release there will be an argument 'cache=FALSE'
so that you have to extractRawCopyNumbers(..., cache=TRUE) if you
really want to cache the results (in memory).

Cheers

Henrik

Plus I believe that you might be missing a step in the above code:
fit(plm, verbose=verbose)

See http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/total-copy-number-analysis-6-0
for details

regards

Lavinia.

messages.subject: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] Aroma took me a long time for processing Affy 6.0 data
messages.subject_clean: [aroma.affymetrix] Aroma took me a long time for processing Affy 6.0 data
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

as Lavinia says, you've forgot to actually fit() the PLM.

Second, please always report your sessionInfo().

Third, could you please be more specific with what you mean by the
"last step"?  Is that

  cesN <- process(fln, verbose=verbose)?

If you read the Vignette 'Total Copy Number Analysis (5.0 & 6.0)' you
find in the end of Section 'PCR fragment length normalization' the
comment "Fragment-length normalization takes approximately 1
min/array", so "four days" and still running for 90 arrays doesn't
sound right.  It could be related to not fitting the PLM, because then
all chip effects are zero and maybe the FLN algorithms doesn't
converge, but that is a bit far fetched.

It would help if you report the verbose output so that we know if
where it "get stuck".  I would use

  verbose <- Arguments$getVerbose(-8);
  timestampOn(verbose);

so that you also get the timing information.

Also, make sure to read the FAQ.

/Henrik

messages.subject: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] Segmentation fault when running GLAD
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I cannot tell what is going wrong, but my guess is that it can be
related to the following NEWS item of R v2.7.0:

SIGNIFICANT USER-VISIBLE CHANGES

    o	Packages which include graphics devices need to be re-installed
	for this version of R, with recently updated versions.

Since you are using R v2.6.1, the Cairo package you've got installed
might be build for R v2.7.0 and not compatible with R v2.7.0.

So, you could test if you can load Cairo and use its PNG device to
generate a PNG file, or simply update to R v2.7.1.

Henrik

messages.subject: Re: How to retrieve the position information
messages.subject_clean: How to retrieve the position information
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm not sure how to do this, but I'm wondering why you want to do
this?
If you follow the flow of an analysis for 5.0 chips, then you will end
up with a list of called regions, with positional information.
Or you could extract the raw copy numbers and then each SNP has a
precise location (this information is available from Affymetrix in
their supplementary data).

cheers

Lavinia.

messages.body_plain:
Markus.

The aroma.affymetrix processing is based on the defaults of affyPLM's
'fitPLM', which is: background.method = "RMA.2" and normalize.method =
"quantile".

Here is a test script that I wrote about a year ago (so take it with a
grain of salt):
http://bioinf.wehi.edu.au/folders/mrobinson/for_hb/u133.test.mark.R

My test was based on the chip effects and they matched up, so
presumably the BG adjustment and normalization also matched.  I
believe a variation of this test is used everytime aroma.affymetrix is
built.  Note I haven't used the 'extractAffyBatch' and I'm not sure if
that introduces any differences in the order, etc.

Sorry, I haven't answered your question as I don't have access to run
my code at the moment ... but hopefully this give you an avenue to
check.

Mark

messages.body_plain:
Further to Mark's email, it is not the probe ordering that is the problem (note that the difference in the background corrected signals is ~ 1e-8), but the following line:

> qn <- QuantileNormalization(cs, typesToAvg="pm")

This is telling aroma.affymetrix to average the quantiles from the PM only to get the target distribution.  However, by default, the normalisation will adjust *all* the signals using the target distribution, not just the PM - hence the difference Markus is seeing.  If this line is changed to

> qn <- QuantileNormalization(cs, typesToUpdate="pm")

then you should see very little difference between the two implementations (~ 1e-5 in the test run I did).  By default, typesToAvg = typesToUpdate and so this call will average the PM quantiles (typesToAvg="pm"), and update *only* the PM signals (typesToUpdate="pm").

(Markus - I'm not sure why you performed background correction but then quantile normalised the unadjusted signals - was this just for testing purposes?)

Cheers,

Ken

> > adjust *all* the signals using the target distribution, not just the PM -
> > hence the difference Markus is seeing.  If this line is changed to

> > > qn <- QuantileNormalization(cs, typesToUpdate="pm")

> > (~ 1e-5 in the test run I did).  By default, typesToAvg = typesToUpdate and

messages.subject: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] working with ax13339 cdf
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I've had a look at the CDF you sent me offline.  I've had a look at
the structure, and although one could guess that it is a CDF for SNP
chip, the structure is totally different from all other Affymetrix SNP
chip CDFs.  None of the methods in aroma.affymetrix for SNP/CN
analysis will work with this CDF structure.  If that is wanted, the
"fastest" approach is to create a new CDF that follows the structure
of all the other SNP chip CDFs.

The dimension of the ax13339 chip type is 712x712, which is also the
dimension of the Mapping10K_Xba131 chip type.  There is a small
possibility that these two chip types are actually identical (same
production masks used) and that it is only the CDFs that differ.  If
so, CDFs for the Mapping10K_Xba131 chip type could be used.  Note
though, that that is just a wild guess/hope and need to be checked
further.  Moreover, all units in the CDF are listed as 'CustomSeq'
units (unit type 1);

cdf <- AffymetrixCdfFile$byChipType("ax13339");
unitTypes <- getUnitTypes(cdf);
table(unitTypes);
unitTypes
    1
10043

and not as 'Genotyping' (unit type 2) as expected if they would be SNP units.

I have at least created a new page for this chip type, where we can
add new information if found:

 http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/ax13339

If anyone else have pointers/references to the origin of the ax13339
CDF, please let me/us know.

Cheers

Henrik

extractMatrix.AffymetrixCelSet<-
function (this, cells = NULL, ..., field = c("intensities", "stdvs",
     "pixels"), verbose = FALSE)
{
     cdf <- getCdf(this)
     if (is.null(cells)) {
         ncells <- nbrOfCells(cdf)
     }
     else {
         cells <- Arguments$getIndices(cells, range = c(1,
nbrOfCells(cdf)))
         ncells <- length(cells)
     }
     field <- match.arg(field)
     verbose <- Arguments$getVerbose(verbose)
     if (verbose) {
         pushState(verbose)
         on.exit(popState(verbose))
     }
     settings <- getOption("aroma.affymetrix.settings")
     gcArrayFrequency <- settings$memory$gcArrayFrequency
     if (is.null(gcArrayFrequency))
         gcArrayFrequency <- 10
     verbose && enter(verbose, "Getting data for the array set")
     verbose && enter(verbose, "Allocating matrix")
     arrayNames <- getNames(this)
     nbrOfArrays <- length(arrayNames)
     df <- matrix(NA, nrow = ncells, ncol = nbrOfArrays)
     colnames(df) <- arrayNames
     verbose && str(verbose, df)
     verbose && printf(verbose, "RAM: %.2fMB\n", object.size(df)/1024^2)
     verbose && exit(verbose)
     if (!is.null(cells)) {
         verbose && enter(verbose, "Optimize reading order")
         o <- order(cells)
         cells <- cells[o]
         #o <- order(o)             #### Mark R added this HERE ####
         verbose && exit(verbose)
     }
     else {
         o <- seq(length = ncells)
     }
     gc <- gc()
     verbose && print(verbose, gc)
     verbose && enter(verbose, "Retrieving data")
     for (aa in seq_len(nbrOfArrays)) {
         verbose && printf(verbose, "Array %d,\n", aa)
         cf <- getFile(this, aa)
         df[o, aa] <- getData(cf, indices = cells, fields = field,
             verbose = less(verbose))[[field]]
         if (aa%%gcArrayFrequency == 0) {
             gc <- gc()
             verbose && print(verbose, gc)
         }
     }
     verbose && exit(verbose)
     verbose && exit(verbose)
     df
}

On Mon, Jun 16, 2008 at 7:07 AM, cstratowa
<Christian...@vie.boehringer-ingelheim.com> wrote:

> Dear Henrik

> chip and create symlinks to directories rawData, annotationData and

> XY,QN,RMA,A+B,FLN,-XY/Mapping250K_Sty/.average-intensities-median-
> mad,def1a76532f24e3899d90fcec50fa3ac.CEL.tmp -> plmData/TestPerl2,ACC,-
> XY,QN,RMA,A+B,FLN,-XY/Mapping250K_Sty/.average-intensities-median-
> mad,def1a76532f24e3899d90fcec50fa3ac.CEL
>
> Can you explain what this error means? When and why  is a temporary
> file created?
> Does  this ".average-intensities-median-mad,xxx.CEL" file contain the
> average intensities of the normalized CEL-files?
> Is there a way to create this ".average-intensities-median-
> mad,xxx.CEL" file with a defined method after normalization, so that
> GLAD "knows" that this average file exists already and does not to try
> to create this file itself?

Yes, that file contains the average of the CEL files in a data set.

It is actually when getAverageFile() of AffymetrixCelSet calls
createFrom() of AffymetrixCelFile, when the temporary file is created
and exists.  In your case, the different hosts happens to be running
createFrom() at the same time.  The createFrom() method creates a
valid CEL files either by copying a template CEL file or creating it
from scratch.  It also takes an argument 'clear' which will make sure
the CEL files has all zeros if clear=TRUE.  If a template CEL file is
used, clear=TRUE has to "update" the CEL with all zeros, if created
from scratch, this is not needed.  However, since createFrom() can be
a two-step process, working with a temporary file is the only way to
"guarantee" that you get what you requested (in case of interrupts
etc).

Ideally, getAverageFile() of AffymetrixCelSet would also work with a
temporary file first and when complete rename it to the final name.
That would the method more "atomic", i.e. either complete or fail.
Right now, I think it is possible to interrupt getAverageFile() and
get a incomplete file.  Yet another thing on the todo list.

/Henrik

>
> Best regards
> Christian
>
>
>
> On Jun 11, 8:37 pm, "Henrik Bengtsson" <h...@stat.berkeley.edu> wrote:
>> Hi Christian,
>>
>> the patch I provided was only for the very basic race conditions in
>> ChromosomeExplorer, but not in preceeding models/algorithms, e.g.
>> GladModel, AvgCnPlm etc.
>>
>> The whole paralizing of aroma.affymetrix (and other computations) is
>> complicated and the only safe solution to deal with race conditions
>> like the ones you are reporting is to work with a semaphore/mutex
>> mechanism.  Such a solution is not available in R and until that it
>> available it does not make sense to put much effort to work around it
>> in aroma.affymetrix.  I don't think the R language itself will provide
>> this feature in a long time.  Instead I think "we" have to to create
>> "mutex" package that provides the necessary features.  The challenges
>> is to make such a package to work on all platforms and more
>> importantly be bullet proof.
>>
>> FYI, I've looked into options like using RSQLite to provide the mutex
>> functionality, but unfortunately it turns out that SQLite itself is
>> not parallel safe and depends heavily on the underlying OS.  It seems
>> that the easiest solution is to have one dedicated server handing out
>> semaphores via a TCP/IP connection (opening and closing connections
>> are race-condition safe to the best of my knowledge).  However, such a
>> solution is not immediately transparent to aroma.affymetrix, so I've
>> procrastinated that path.  One can also work with lock files as
>> semaphores, but they are not bullet proof and there are cases where
>> two processes can lock the same file - it is better than nothing but
>> not safe.
>>
>> To summarize, don't expect parallel computation in aroma.affymetrix
>> until there exist a well tested "mutex" package in R.
>>
>> Cheers
>>
>> Henrik

messages.subject: Re: aroma.affymetrix and affy - different results
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

here are some more details on what Ken says:

The QuantileNormalization(cs, ...) method in aroma.affymetrix
normalizes each array separately toward a target distribution.

If not specified explicitly, the target distribution is calculated as
the average sort():ed and approx():ed intensities across all arrays in
the data set. The details can be found in averageQuantile() for the
AffymetrixCelSet class.  The algorithm is the same as
aroma.light::averageQuantile() for the 'list' class, which was adopted
from 'limma' in 2002 and 2006 (which to the best of my knowledge
originates from Ben Bolstad's first implementation).  See
print(aroma.light::averageQuantile.list) for details.

The normalization toward the target distribution is then done using
aroma.light::normalizeQuantile(), which also was adopted from 'limma'
(with the same ancestors etc).  See
print(aroma.light::normalizeQuantileRank.numeric) for details.

I haven't followed development of the limma version, but I'd say they
give very similar, if not all.equal(), results.

Finally, another reason for the observed differences may be
differences in precision.  The output from QuantileNormalization is
stored in CEL files, where probe intensities are stored as floats (4
bytes).  Normalized data held in memory are doubles (8 bytes), which
is the case for most Bioconductor packages.

FYI, one of the redundancy tests being run before every major release
of aroma.affymetrix, verifies that aroma.affymetrix
(RmaBackgroundCorrection + QuantileNormalization + RmaPlm) can
reproduce the RMA
chip-effect estimates as estimated by affyPLM (mean/sd squared
differences < 10^-4).  The test was adopted from the script that Mark
Robinson posted earlier.

Cheers

/Henrik

> > chip and create symlinks to directories rawData, annotationData and
> > later to plmData.

> > XY,QN,RMA,A+B,FLN,-XY/Mapping250K_Sty/.average-intensities-median-
> > mad,def1a76532f24e3899d90fcec50fa3ac.CEL.tmp -> plmData/TestPerl2,ACC,-

>
> > Can you explain what this error means? When and why  is a temporary
> > file created?
> > Does  this ".average-intensities-median-mad,xxx.CEL" file contain the
> > average intensities of the normalized CEL-files?
> > Is there a way to create this ".average-intensities-median-
> > mad,xxx.CEL" file with a defined method after normalization, so that
> > GLAD "knows" that this average file exists already and does not to try
> > to create this file itself?
>
> Yes, that file contains the average of the CEL files in a data set.
>
> It is actually when getAverageFile() of AffymetrixCelSet calls
> createFrom() of AffymetrixCelFile, when the temporary file is created
> and exists.  In your case, the different hosts happens to be running
> createFrom() at the same time.  The createFrom() method creates a
> valid CEL files either by copying a template CEL file or creating it
> from scratch.  It also takes an argument 'clear' which will make sure
> the CEL files has all zeros if clear=TRUE.  If a template CEL file is
> used, clear=TRUE has to "update" the CEL with all zeros, if created
> from scratch, this is not needed.  However, since createFrom() can be
> a two-step process, working with a temporary file is the only way to
> "guarantee" that you get what you requested (in case of interrupts
> etc).
>
> Ideally, getAverageFile() of AffymetrixCelSet would also work with a
> temporary file first and when complete rename it to the final name.
> That would the method more "atomic", i.e. either complete or fail.
> Right now, I think it is possible to interrupt getAverageFile() and
> get a incomplete file.  Yet another thing on the todo list.
>
> /Henrik
>
>
>
>
>
> > Best regards
> > Christian
>
> > On Jun 11, 8:37 pm, "Henrik Bengtsson" <h...@stat.berkeley.edu> wrote:
> >> Hi Christian,
>
> >> the patch I provided was only for the very basic race conditions in
> >> ChromosomeExplorer, but not in preceeding models/algorithms, e.g.
> >> GladModel, AvgCnPlm etc.
>
> >> The whole paralizing of aroma.affymetrix (and other computations) is
> >> complicated and the only safe solution to deal with race conditions
> >> like the ones you are reporting is to work with a semaphore/mutex
> >> mechanism.  Such a solution is not available in R and until that it
> >> available it does not make sense to put much effort to work around it
> >> in aroma.affymetrix.  I don't think the R language itself will provide
> >> this feature in a long time.  Instead I think "we" have to to create
> >> "mutex" package that provides the necessary features.  The challenges
> >> is to make such a package to work on all platforms and more
> >> importantly be bullet proof.
>
> >> FYI, I've looked into options like using RSQLite to provide the mutex
> >> functionality, but unfortunately it turns out that SQLite itself is
> >> not parallel safe and depends heavily on the underlying OS.  It seems
> >> that the easiest solution is to have one dedicated server handing out
> >> semaphores via a TCP/IP connection (opening and closing connections
> >> are race-condition safe to the best of my knowledge).  However, such a
> >> solution is not immediately transparent to aroma.affymetrix, so I've
> >> procrastinated that path.  One can also work with lock files as
> >> semaphores, but they are not bullet proof and there are cases where
> >> two processes can lock the same file - it is better than nothing but
> >> not safe.
>
> >> To summarize, don't expect parallel computation in aroma.affymetrix
> >> until there exist a well tested "mutex" package in R.
>
> >> Cheers
>
> >> Henrik

It is hard to compare this figures with the 338 array data set,
because of the differ chunk sizes etc.  However, from even from the
above 22 array data set, it looks to me that you spend a fair bit of
time (62.7%) in reading the data.  If you compare this to what you get
if you work toward a local drive, you'll probably see that it will be
much faster.  Note that the "writing" fraction is mostly spend in the
unwrapping/wrapping (encoding/writing) part, and not per se for the
actual writing to file.  The writing to file is very roughly
(100-71.24)% of 29.6%.

Another reason for the processing time of 338 arrays seems
"exponentially" slower than for 22 arrays, could be that there are
more file-cache misses when more files (and more disk space) have to
be accessed in each chunk.  With 22 arrays, the file cache might get
more read/write cache hits.

>> earlier threads, handling the single-probe CN units separately by
>> immediately transfer their intensities to chip effects would speed up
>> things a lot.  If done correctly, that will come down to copying
>> values from the input CEL files to the output chip-effect CEL files;
>> right now those are processed through the complete PLM fitting
>> mechanism.
>
> This sounds interesting.
> Could you be more specific, since I am afraid that I do not quite
> understand what you mean?

See the thread 'Parallelizing the Total Copy Number Analysis (GWS6)
Options' and my reply on April 8, 2008.

In order to do this, it is important to understand how the PLM
model(s) work.  When you do that you will also understand that there
are no probe-affinity parameters to fit for the single-probe units, so
the whole modeling vanishes.  This will lead you to a simple "model"
where the chip-effect estimate of a single-probe CN units is identical
to the intensity of the CN probe.  Thus, you can just copy the value
over regardless of PLM.

> Is there also a possibility for me to do things in parallel?

Yes, but that should not be the first goal.  The main gain will be the
skipping of the fitting mechanism for all CN probes (which are 50% of
the units on the new arrays).

>> bytesPerChunk <- 100e6;
>> unitsPerChunk <- ram * bytesPerChunk / bytesPerUnit;
>
> Would setting e.g. "moreUnits=10" increase the processing speed?
> Does "moreUnits=10" need only 1GB RAM or more?

Use the 'ram' argument instead.  The 'moreUnits' argument is obsolete
and there for backward compatibility.

The 'bytesPerChunk' is just a scaling constant.  Don't consider it an
estimate of the number of bytes per chunk, at most a number
proportional to the number of bytes per chunk, but it depends a lot on
the fitting algorithm called and that varies with PLMs (and
'flavor':s).  It also depends on the number of probes in a unit, which
depends on the specific CDF etc.  So you cannot really predict the
number bytes.

Anyway, if you use ram > 1, more units per chunk will be fitted, and
with ram < 1, less units per will be fitted, than what is the default
(ram = 1).  So, if you see that you are not using all of your RAM, you
can increase the 'ram' argument.  This will use more memory.  It will
also decrease the I/O overhead of opening and closing files for
reading, because this is done fewer times when there are less chunks.
In each chunk, a larger portion of the CEL files are also
read/writing, which will improve the I/O speed *per unit* as well (the
reason/details are in affxparser::updateCel()).  However, I think
there are properties that also vary with hardware system and file
system.  My guts tells me though that a larger value of 'ram' will
speed up things.  There is probably an upper limit when the marginal
gain vanish.  Basically it is a trial an error to find out.  You're
welcome to post some summary data here, if you do a comparison.

Cheers

Henrik

> > Would setting e.g. "moreUnits=10" increase the processing speed?
> > Does "moreUnits=10" need only 1GB RAM or more?
>
> Use the 'ram' argument instead.  The 'moreUnits' argument is obsolete
> and there for backward compatibility.
>
> The 'bytesPerChunk' is just a scaling constant.  Don't consider it an
> estimate of the number of bytes per chunk, at most a number
> proportional to the number of bytes per chunk, but it depends a lot on
> the fitting algorithm called and that varies with PLMs (and
> 'flavor':s).  It also depends on the number of probes in a unit, which
> depends on the specific CDF etc.  So you cannot really predict the
> number bytes.
>
> Anyway, if you use ram > 1, more units per chunk will be fitted, and
> with ram < 1, less units per will be fitted, than what is the default
> (ram = 1).  So, if you see that you are not using all of your RAM, you
> can increase the 'ram' argument.  This will use more memory.  It will
> also decrease the I/O overhead of opening and closing files for
> reading, because this is done fewer times when there are less chunks.
> In each chunk, a larger portion of the CEL files are also
> read/writing, which will improve the I/O speed *per unit* as well (the
> reason/details are in affxparser::updateCel()).  However, I think
> there are properties that also vary with hardware system and file
> system.  My guts tells me though that a larger value of 'ram' will
> speed up things.  There is probably an upper limit when the marginal
> gain vanish.  Basically it is a trial an error to find out.  You're
> welcome to post some summary data here, if you do a comparison.
>
> Cheers
>

messages.subject: Re: Processing problem with RmaCnPlm() for 338 samples
messages.subject_clean: Processing problem with RmaCnPlm() for 338 samples
messages.body_plain:
Dear Henrik

Luckily this turned out to be an artifact. Since I am writing the
output to a text-file, it seems that I opened the incomplete text-file
just when the program tried to write, causing these artifacts.

Now, that the computation finished I can give you the results of
fitting PLM for 85 samples, when using a server with 32GB RAM as
cluster node:

Fitting model of class RmaCnPlm:...

...
 Fitting chunk #102 of 102...done
 Total time for all units across all 85 arrays: 5617.77s == 93.63min
 Total time per unit across all 85 arrays: 0.02s/unit
 Total time per unit and array: 0.277ms/unit & array
 Total time for one array (238378 units): 1.10min = 0.02h
 Total time for complete data set: 93.63min = 1.56h
 Fraction of time spent on different tasks: Fitting: 12.6%, Reading:
25.5%, Writing: 60.6% (of which 83.67% is for encoding/writing chip-
effects), Explicit garbage collection: 1.2%

Fitting model of class RmaCnPlm:...done

As you see, fitting 85 samples needed only 1.5hrs, which is fine.
Nevertheles, I will try to increase parameter "ram".
In comparison, fitting 22 samples on a typical cluster node needed
already 1.6hrs, while fitting 48 samples on a typical cluster node
needed 5.7hrs, although writing to the same network drive!

Thus the take-home message seems to be:
Do not use a typical cluster node (in our case 2 CPUs with 1GB RAM
shared memory) for PLM-fitting.
(First experience shows that even nodes with 4 CPUs and 8GB shared
memory may not be sufficient)

One more info:
The main reason for using a cluster was to run GLAD in parallel. In
this case the processing time was:
For 85 samples using Nsp-Sty GLAD needed about 140min/node.
For 48 samples using only Sty GLAD needed about 30min/node.

Best regards
Christian

the chip you are using.

messages.subject: PCR fragment length normalization
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

This question may be more specific for the Bengtsson et. al. 2008
paper. I'm not sure, but I think it will be fine to post it here
because it also regards the aroma.affymetrix normalization model.

I have read the paper and I wonder if the the Calculation of Raw copy
numbers eq(12) could accomodate
the fragment length correction eq(10).
And more importantly, the question is: Could the median itself eq(13)
as well compensate the Fragment length effect making the FLN step
redundant?
Maybe I'm missing something but the only problem I see in skipping the
FLN is that the median may not be robust enough to correct FL in the
presence of CN alteration on those probes.

Regarding the FLN implemented in the aroma.affymetrix for the SNP6.0
arrays is the same as in the paper?
I read the documentation and it says that it will be detailed in a
future paper, but I would like to know some
details now about the model ... :) if it is possible, a high level
description...

I will really appreciate your time and effort,

Roger,

messages.subject: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] PCR fragment length normalization
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

On Mon, Jul 14, 2008 at 5:39 PM, Roger <rpi...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi,
>
> This question may be more specific for the Bengtsson et. al. 2008
> paper. I'm not sure, but I think it will be fine to post it here
> because it also regards the aroma.affymetrix normalization model.
>
>
> I have read the paper and I wonder if the the Calculation of Raw copy
> numbers eq(12) could accomodate
> the fragment length correction eq(10).
> And more importantly, the question is: Could the median itself eq(13)
> as well compensate the Fragment length effect making the FLN step
> redundant?
> Maybe I'm missing something but the only problem I see in skipping the
> FLN is that the median may not be robust enough to correct FL in the
> presence of CN alteration on those probes.

your question is a valid question.  In Eqn (10) of Bengtsson et al.
(2008), we write the fragment-length normalization as:

  log2(theta*_ij) = log2(theta^_ij) - delta^_ij

where theta*_ij is the normalized chip effect for sample i=1,2,...,I
and locus/SNP/unit j=1,2,...,J.  Continuing, theta^_ij is the
estimated chip effect (from the PLM), and delta^_ij is the estimated
fragment-length effect for that sample and that locus.  Note that we
estimate the FL effect for each array, hence index 'i'.

So, to your point, when calculating the log-ratios as in Eqn (12);

  M_ij = log2(theta*_ij / theta*_Rj) = log2(theta*_ij) - log2(theta*_Rj)

where theta*_Rj is the robust average of several samples, the FL
normalized data evaluates as:

  M_ij = [log2(theta^_ij) - delta^_ij] - [log2(theta^_Rj) - delta^_Rj]
         = [log2(theta^_ij/theta^_Rj) - [delta^_ij - delta^_Rj].

Note that *if and only if* fragment-length effect is the same for
sample 'i' and reference 'R', then delta^_ij - delta^_Rj == 0, and the
effect should cancel out.

However, whenever there is a small difference, then the
fragment-length effect will carry through to the log ratios.  You can
see this yourself.  If you plot log2(theta) versus fragment length and
draw a lowess or smooth spline through the data points you will find
that the longer fragments have less signal.  You can see an example on
Page 'Calibration And Normalization Of Summarized Data'
[http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/calibration-and-normalization-of-summarized-data].
 Now if you do this for many arrays, you will find that there are
small differences in the fitted curves across arrays.

To summarize: We do expect to see a fragment-length effect in our
theta:s - that is not strange and we do not remove that effect, we
only make the effect the same across all arrays (we normalize towards
the "target").  When we have made the effect the same for all arrays,
then it will cancel out as you suggest.  One could of course generate
log ratios and normalize those (as in Nannya et al. 2005), but it more
practical to not bring in a reference until the very end.

>
>
> Regarding the FLN implemented in the aroma.affymetrix for the SNP6.0
> arrays is the same as in the paper?
> I read the documentation and it says that it will be detailed in a
> future paper, but I would like to know some
> details now about the model ... :) if it is possible, a high level
> description...

That work is still to be written up, but the issue with the newer GWS5
& GWS6 chip types is that DNA digested in parallel by two different
enzymes are hybridized to the same array.  This means that the
observed signals are affected by two different fragment-length
effects.  We use a simple mixture model to estimate the two effects
and correct for them.  For simplicity you can think of extending Eqn
(10) so it has two delta^_ij terms.

Cheers

Henrik

>
> I will really appreciate your time and effort,
>
> Roger,
>
>
>
>
>
>
> >
>

anything, but don't worry if you can't send it.

Thank you very much again,

Roger,

messages.subject: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] Running GLAD on three separate normalization runs?
messages.subject_clean: [aroma.affymetrix] Running GLAD on three separate normalization runs?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I've just got an offline reminder that this one wasn't answered yet.

On Wed, Jun 18, 2008 at 3:03 PM, Uri David Akavia
<uridavi...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi.
>
> I'm trying to process multiple batches.
> Two batches are tumor samples, one batch is normal samples (they are
> not paired, but I have a large amount of normal samples).

One question is if you really want process them separately or
together.  You are asking how to do it separately so I will answer
that below, but in case you want to combine two or more raw data sets
and then carry on with them as if they are one, you just do:

cs1 <- AffymetrixCelSet$fromName(dataSets[1], cdf=cdf);
cs2 <- AffymetrixCelSet$fromName(dataSets[2], cdf=cdf);
cs3 <- AffymetrixCelSet$fromName(dataSets[3], cdf=cdf);

cs <- clone(cs1);
append(cs, cs2);
append(cs, cs3);
rm(cs1, cs2, cs3); # Not needed anymore

When you then process the data, the full name of the output data set
will be the same as the fullname of 'cs', i.e. getFullName(cs).  This
is the same as the name of the first data set you added, i.e.
getFullName(cs1).  [In the next release of the package there will a
way to change the output name].

The rest of my reply will explain how to processes data sets
separately and then merge then at the very end.

> I processed each using cRMA, where I used the following commands (on
> each batch separately):
>
> cs <- AffymetrixCelSet$fromName("glioma,testSet",cdf=cdf)
> print(cs)
> acc <- AllelicCrosstalkCalibration(cs)
> print(acc)
> csC <- process(acc, verbose=verbose)
> print(csC)
> plm <- AvgCnPlm(csC, mergeStrands=TRUE, combineAlleles=TRUE, shift=
> +300)
> print(plm)
> fit(plm, verbose=verbose)
> ces <- getChipEffectSet(plm)
> print(ces)
> fln <- FragmentLengthNormalization(ces)
> print(fln)
> cesN <- process(fln, verbose=verbose)
> print(cesN)
>
> I kept the data analysis of each batch (Normal, Tumor1, Tumor2) in
> different directories, where the subdirectories of plm, acc and so on
> were created in each directory separately.
> Therefore my data structure looks like this
> DATA/Normal/plmData
> DATA/Tumor1/plmData

So, instead of using different working directories, in your case
DATA/Normal/ and DATA/Tumor/, I would recommend that you use the same
working directory for all your analysis.  That should for most people
and that is how aroma.affymetrix is designed.  If you do that, your
processed data will be outputted in the same probeData/, the same
plmData/ and so on.  That is much more convinient.

>
> I now have separate cesN, and I would like to run GLAD, comparing the
> two batches of tumor samples to the normal samples.
> Each cesN object has a path, which I can see by doing getPath(cesN),
> for example
> getPath(cesN)
> [1] "plmData/glioma,testSet,ACC,ra,-XY,AVG,+300,A+B,FLN,-XY/
> GenomeWideSNP_6"
>
> I think I need to change the path, so it includes the dir before I run
> GLAD (so it will become "Normal/plmData/glioma,testSet,ACC,ra,-XY,AVG,
> +300,A+B,FLN,-XY/GenomeWideSNP_6"). Is this correct?

No.

> If so, how do I do that? I tried searching for a command called
> setPath(), but couldn't find it.

So, you don't want to do that, because that is against how
aroma.affymetrix is designed and supposed to be used; you should not
have to specify absolute paths, actually not even relative paths.  If
your analysis scripts contain a path you are probably doing something
wrong.

It looks from you description that your two data sets have the same
names, that is, if you do getFullName(cs) in the two cases you get the
identical names: "glioma,testSet".  You do not want to this, because
two data sets should not have the same full name if they are actually
different.

So, this is the setup I would suggest you to use.  I'm not sure if the
tag 'testSet' is important to you or not, but I keep here as an
example:

rawData/
  glioma1,testSet/
    GenomeWideSNP_6/
       *.CEL
  glioma2,testSet/
    GenomeWideSNP_6/
       *.CEL
  MyNormalDataSet/
    GenomeWideSNP_6/
       *.CEL

I strongly recommend, and ask you to please read the 'User Guide'
online [http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/users-guide],
and especially the first few section on the setup of directories etc.
Try to get a feel of the design of the package.  If there is anything
unclear or ambiguous, please let us know how we can clarify it.

With the above rawData, you can process the two data sets like this:

verbose <- Arguments$getVerbose(-8, timestamp=TRUE);

# Setup the annotation data
cdf <- AffymetrixCdfFile$byChipType("GenomeWideSNP_6", tags="Full");

dataSets <- c("glioma1,testSet", "glioma2,testSet", "MyNormalDataSet");
cs <- AffymetrixCelSet$fromName(dataSets[1], cdf=cdf);
print(cs);

acc <- AllelicCrosstalkCalibration(cs);
print(acc);
csC <- process(acc, verbose=verbose);

print(csC);

Repeating the above for all data sets separately would generate
normalized data sets:

probeData/
  glioma1,testSet,ACC,,ra-XY/
  glioma2,testSet,ACC,,ra-XY/
  MyNormalDataSet,ACC,,ra-XY/

plm <- AvgCnPlm(csC, mergeStrands=TRUE, combineAlleles=TRUE, shift=+300);

print(plm);
fit(plm, verbose=verbose);
ces <- getChipEffectSet(plm);

print(ces);

Repeating the above for all data sets separately would generate chip
effect sets:

plmData/
  glioma1,testSet,ACC,,ra-XY,AVG,+300,A+B/
  glioma2,testSet,ACC,,ra-XY,AVG,+300,A+B/
  MyNormalDataSet,ACC,,ra-XY,AVG,+300,A+B/

fln <- FragmentLengthNormalization(ces);
print(fln);
cesN <- process(fln, verbose=verbose);

print(cesN);

Repeating the above for all data sets separately would generate
normalized chip effect sets:

plmData/
  glioma1,testSet,ACC,,ra-XY,AVG,+300,A+B,FLN,-XY/
  glioma2,testSet,ACC,,ra-XY,AVG,+300,A+B,FLN,-XY/
  MyNormalDataSet,ACC,,ra-XY,AVG,+300,A+B,FLN,-XY/

If you do not want to process all your data again, you can rename all
dataset directories in probeData/, plmData/ etc accordingly and put
move the to the same place as above.  That is safe to do.

>
> How should I merge the results from each separate normalization, so I
> can run GLAD comparing the two tumor batches to normal files?

It sounds like you can/want to treat the two tumor data sets
separately, and that you want to compare each tumor to the pool of the
normals, correct.  Let's assume that your chip effects for the tumor
data set is 'cesN' and the chip effects for the normals is 'cesNRef'.
Then do:

# Calculate the average *file* of all fragment-length normalized chip
effects for the normals.
ceR <- getAverageFile(cesNRef, verbose=verbose);

# You then have to fake a reference *data set* containing this file replicate
cesR <- newInstance(cesN, rep(list(ceR), nbrOfArrays(cesN)));

# Setup the GLAD segmentation model
glad <- GladModel(cesN, cesR);

and process as "usual".

Hope this helps

Henrik

>
> Thank you very much,
>
> Uri David Akavia
> >
>

messages.body_plain:
Hi Alex,

On Thu, Jul 17, 2008 at 1:41 PM, Alex Lisovich <alex.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Dear List,
>
> I am very new to the field of CNV analysis and aroma package so please
> forgive me for naive questions.
> I am running the paired analysis as described in tutorial. It seems
> that there is a typo in paired analysis code sample, specifically in
> "PCR fragment length normalization" instead of:
>
> cesFlnList <- list();
> for (chipType in names(csList)) {
>  ces <- cesCnList[[chipType]];
>  fln <- FragmentLengthNormalization(ces);
>  print(fln);
>  cesFln <- process(fln, verbose=log);
>  cesFlnList[[chipType]] <- cesFln;
> }
>
> it should read:
>
> cesFlnList <- list();
> for (chipType in names(cesList)) {
>  ces <- cesList[[chipType]];
>  fln <- FragmentLengthNormalization(ces);
>  print(fln);
>  cesFln <- process(fln, verbose=log);
>  cesFlnList[[chipType]] <- cesFln;
> }
>
> otherwise it will  not run due to the name mismatch with the previous
> ("Summarization") section.

thanks for reporting these typos.  The vignette has been updated.

>
> After this fix it works and the result of chr.20 for tumor-normal pair
> (CRL-5868D, CRL-5957D) is the same as in the vignette,
> but I have the difficulty interpreting the results: it seems that big
> chunks of output signal  (for example, CRL-2324D vs CRL-2325D, chr.
> 1,2,3)
> have a  shift of a mean value by a fraction of a unity copy number
> relative to each other and I am wondering if this a physical or
> processing artifact?

The first and most important comment is that you cannot and should not
interpret the log2 ratios as true/real log2 copy numbers.  There are
many reasons for this, but one is that the microarray technology does
not measure the underlying copy number on a linear (proportional)
scale, e.g. if you double the CN the observed signal is not doubled.
What holds is that large CNs have large log-ratios and vice verse.
This comment applies to all CN data sets.

Different methods have been proposed to calibrate the log2 ratios
("raw CNs") toward know CN levels so that can interpret the log2
ratios as true log2 ratios.  This kind of calibration can be done
after normalizing the chip effects (e.g. fragment-length
normalization).  Doing this kind of calibration will only have little
impact on the segmentation, i.e. you will in practice find the same
breakpoints in both cases (except maybe for some extremely short noise
regions).

I don't know the details about this particular data set, but it is
quite likely that the tumor sample is contaminated by normal cells as
well (very common), which will cause us compare a mixture of tumor and
normals towards normals.  That would further explain (true) CN levels
that are not 0, 1, 2, ...  Furthermore, if the tumor sample is not
only contaminated by normal cells but also by other kind of tumor
cells that have different CN aberrations, you can get very complicated
regions.

> I've learned from the previous discussions on the list that running
> tumor sample against the large enough reference set would remove it
> through normalization,. but still what  process
> would cause such a shift in a paired analysis?

Using a large set of pure normals as a reference is only like have a
single normal sample with very little noise.  The more normals you
average over, the less noisy your reference becomes.  It does not
affect the CN levels of the reference though.  It should reflect CN=2
at all positions (except possibly for common CN polymorphic regions).
 Having a small number of normals in the reference will typically just
add noise, but it is unlikely that it will "introduce" CN regions.

>  I thought that
> neighboring SNPs are scattered across the chip so it should not be a
> local chip luminance variance.

Each SNP contain multiple probes (except the single CN probes on the
newer arrays).  These probes are never placed close to each other.
Instead they are spread out spatially on the array to minimize the
risk that one SNP will be biased by spatial artifacts.  Furthermore,
neighboring SNPs on the genome are not placed next to each other on
the array.  I don't know if Affymetrix have done a randomization for
this explicitly, but their standard probe position algorithm is likely
to introduce such a "semi-randomization".

> I would greatly appreciate a brief explanation of this phenomenon.

Hope this helps.  If not, I suggest that you continue this
non-aroma.affymetrix specific question on Bioconductor where more
people can pitch in.

Cheers

Henrik

>
> Thank you
>
> Alex Lisovich
> University of Pittsburgh, DBMI
> 200 Meyran Ave
>
> >

On Jul 17, 5:05 pm, "Henrik Bengtsson" <h...@stat.berkeley.edu> wrote:
> Hi Alex,
>
>
>
> On Thu, Jul 17, 2008 at 1:41 PM, Alex Lisovich <alex.lisov...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> > Dear List,
>
> > I am very new to the field of CNV analysis and aroma package so please
> > forgive me for naive questions.
> > I am running the paired analysis as described in tutorial. It seems
> > that there is a typo in paired analysis code sample, specifically in
> > "PCR fragment length normalization" instead of:
>
> > cesFlnList <- list();
> > for (chipType in names(csList)) {
> >  ces <- cesCnList[[chipType]];
> >  fln <- FragmentLengthNormalization(ces);
> >  print(fln);
> >  cesFln <- process(fln, verbose=log);
> >  cesFlnList[[chipType]] <- cesFln;
> > }
>
> > it should read:
>
> > cesFlnList <- list();
> > for (chipType in names(cesList)) {
> >  ces <- cesList[[chipType]];
> >  fln <- FragmentLengthNormalization(ces);
> >  print(fln);
> >  cesFln <- process(fln, verbose=log);
> >  cesFlnList[[chipType]] <- cesFln;
> > }
>
> > otherwise it will  not run due to the name mismatch with the previous
> > ("Summarization") section.
>
> thanks for reporting these typos.  The vignette has been updated.
>
>
>
> > After this fix it works and the result of chr.20 for tumor-normal pair
> > (CRL-5868D, CRL-5957D) is the same as in the vignette,
> > but I have the difficulty interpreting the results: it seems that big
> > chunks of output signal  (for example, CRL-2324D vs CRL-2325D, chr.
> > 1,2,3)
> > have a  shift of a mean value by a fraction of a unity copy number
> > relative to each other and I am wondering if this a physical or
> > processing artifact?
>
> The first and most important comment is that you cannot and should not
> interpret the log2 ratios as true/real log2 copy numbers.  There are
> many reasons for this, but one is that the microarray technology does
> not measure the underlying copy number on a linear (proportional)
> scale, e.g. if you double the CN the observed signal is not doubled.
> What holds is that large CNs have large log-ratios and vice verse.
> This comment applies to all CN data sets.
>
> Different methods have been proposed to calibrate the log2 ratios
> ("raw CNs") toward know CN levels so that can interpret the log2
> ratios as true log2 ratios.  This kind of calibration can be done
> after normalizing the chip effects (e.g. fragment-length
> normalization).  Doing this kind of calibration will only have little
> impact on the segmentation, i.e. you will in practice find the same
> breakpoints in both cases (except maybe for some extremely short noise
> regions).
>
> I don't know the details about this particular data set, but it is
> quite likely that the tumor sample is contaminated by normal cells as
> well (very common), which will cause us compare a mixture of tumor and
> normals towards normals.  That would further explain (true) CN levels
> that are not 0, 1, 2, ...  Furthermore, if the tumor sample is not
> only contaminated by normal cells but also by other kind of tumor
> cells that have different CN aberrations, you can get very complicated
> regions.
>
> > I've learned from the previous discussions on the list that running
> > tumor sample against the large enough reference set would remove it
> > through normalization,. but still what  process
> > would cause such a shift in a paired analysis?
>
> Using a large set of pure normals as a reference is only like have a
> single normal sample with very little noise.  The more normals you
> average over, the less noisy your reference becomes.  It does not
> affect the CN levels of the reference though.  It should reflect CN=2
> at all positions (except possibly for common CN polymorphic regions).
>  Having a small number of normals in the reference will typically just
> add noise, but it is unlikely that it will "introduce" CN regions.
>
> >  I thought that
> > neighboring SNPs are scattered across the chip so it should not be a
> > local chip luminance variance.
>
> Each SNP contain multiple probes (except the single CN probes on the
> newer arrays).  These probes are never placed close to each other.
> Instead they are spread out spatially on the array to minimize the
> risk that one SNP will be biased by spatial artifacts.  Furthermore,
> neighboring SNPs on the genome are not placed next to each other on
> the array.  I don't know if Affymetrix have done a randomization for
> this explicitly, but their standard probe position algorithm is likely
> to introduce such a "semi-randomization".
>
> > I would greatly appreciate a brief explanation of this phenomenon.
>
> Hope this helps.  If not, I suggest that you continue this
> non-aroma.affymetrix specific question on Bioconductor where more
> people can pitch in.
>
> Cheers
>
> Henrik
>
>
>
> > Thank you
>
> > Alex Lisovich
> > University of Pittsburgh, DBMI
> > 200 Meyran Ave

messages.body_plain:
Hello All,

We have recently started a small project using the custom canine SNP
arrays developed by the Broad Institute. (http://www.broad.mit.edu/
mammals/dog/caninearrayfaq.html - array version 2.) Making chromosome
copy number calls is our first goal. We don't have any 'normal' copy
number samples at this point, can we even make the calls without this
reference?

They give the proper CDF file but as I understand it we will also need
the UGP and UFL files. The problem is that I don't think they exist
because this is a custom chip. Do we actually need them and if so
could they be created from the other files available on their web
page? (AffyV2_all_probeset.txt and v2.feature-response.txt)

Thanks in advance for any help, advice or tips!

-karl

I'm no expert on SNP array analysis, but I understand that using the
robust average of the data set as a reference sample may be an option

following the last /) you can do a search for UFL and/or UGP and you

>

> On Sat, Jul 19, 2008 at 5:26 AM, Karl Dykema <karl....@gmail.com> wrote:
>>
>> We have recently started a small project using the custom canine SNP
>> arrays developed by the Broad Institute. (http://www.broad.mit.edu/
>> mammals/dog/caninearrayfaq.html - array version 2.) Making chromosome
>> copy number calls is our first goal. We don't have any 'normal' copy
>> number samples at this point, can we even make the calls without this
>> reference?
>
> I'm no expert on SNP array analysis, but I understand that using the
> robust average of the data set as a reference sample may be an option
> for you.  Please see the vignette on Total Copy Number Analysis for
> the 10K, 100K, 500K human chips:
> http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/total-copy-number-analysis.

Yes, as Ken says, if you have enough arrays and you can assume that at
any locus more than 50% (theoretically) are copy neutral, the robust
average (median) at that locus will be an estimator of the
copy-neutral mean.

I don't know how many arrays you've got, but the more you have the
better, not only for the above issue but also got get less noise
estimates.  A bit more than two years ago I was asked to do CN
analysis on 3(!) 500K arrays.  The obvious was to go and download the
public HapMap samples and use those as a pooled reference.  However,
it turned out that when more *in-house* hybridizations were produced
they were much better suited as a reference than the outside-produced
HapMap data.  Already 10-15 in-house "unknown" (CN aberrant) arrays
were better than 270 HapMap samples as a reference!  So, collect as
much Canine SNP hybridizations as possible from the same microarray
facility.

>
>> They give the proper CDF file but as I understand it we will also need
>> the UGP and UFL files. The problem is that I don't think they exist
>> because this is a custom chip. Do we actually need them and if so
>> could they be created from the other files available on their web
>> page? (AffyV2_all_probeset.txt and v2.feature-response.txt)
>
> As far as I know, you will definitely need UGP and UFL files.  If you
> go to the main group page (same as the above URL, but without the bit
> following the last /) you can do a search for UFL and/or UGP and you
> should be able to find several discussions or documentation pages
> which should give you enough information to build your own.

You will need the UGP file for the segmentation, because they contain
(chromosome, position) information.  However, you can do without the
UFL file, which contains fragment-length information.  The UFL file is
used for the fragment-length normalization, and we have shown that it
boost the signal, but you will still get decent results without it.

So, I had a look at the DogSty06m520431 (aka "Canine SNP v2") chip
type and what annotation data is available.  I could not locate any
fragment-length information, so for now you have to live without the
UFL file/FragmentLengthNormalization.  However, the
'AffyV2_all_probeset.txt' file contains (chromosome, position)
information, so I create UGP files for both the full size CDF and the
"Platinum" CDF.  I've made them available on the new chip type page
'DogSty06m520431' at:

  http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/dogsty06m520431

Note the comment that you should rename the "Platinum" CDF.  FYI,
there is also a code example at the bottom on how to create the UGP
files from scratch.

Let us know how it goes.

Henrik

messages.subject: Re: Aroma took me a long time for processing Affy 6.0 data
messages.subject_clean: Aroma took me a long time for processing Affy 6.0 data
messages.body_plain:
Sorry I was out of town for several days.

We ran Aroma on a computer cluster powered by Rocks OS. In the cluster
there are 10 computational nodes, 50 cores and a file server. At the
beginning,  we submitted one job (one plate, about 90 subjects) into
one core, and so there are about 50 jobs were running at the same
time. Each job has to copy the files from the file server and has to
write CEL files back to the file server. So, the I/O became the
bottleneck of the whole system because for plm fir, about 60% time is
due to I/O. We ran 50 jobs for 10 days and no results came out.

We finally decided that this was due to I/O issue. So, we copied the
files for each job to the local machines and wrote the results to the
local machine too. After all jobs finished, we collected the CEL files
from local drives. Each job took about 15 hours! This is great!

Suggestion:
    (1) If you run Aroma in a cluster, we suggest that you let Aroma
access data from local drives instead of file server.
    (2) If you run Aroma in a single machine with multiple cores, e.g.
four cores or eight cores, don't be greedy to run four or eight jobs
at the same time. Based on the I/O performance of your computer,
submit at most 2 jobs (based on my experience).

Jerry.

> total-copy-numbers-manually" to calculate raw copy numbers (CNs) from
> chip effect estimates by first "extracting" the chip effects and then
> taking the log2 ratios. This method will return a matrix (number probe
> by number of subjects). I think this matrix is based on the normalized
> CEL files not based on the original CEL files.

Note that "probe" is typically referring to the single features/cells
on the Affymetrix arrays.  The methods you are referring to return
chip effects/raw CNs for units (the same as SNPs on the 10K-500K
arrays).  A unit consists of multiple probes.  If you do total copy
number analysis (which I think you do), then each chip effect estimate
is a *summary* of the probes in a unit, that is, there is one chip
effect per unit and not per probe.

>
>    What I am wondering is if I could extract a similar matrix for the
> plate of subjects, but based on the original CEL files? We would like
> to know the effect of normalization on detecting CNVs.

I am still not sure what you are asking for.  Exactly what do you
refer to when you say "normalization"?  There are both probe-level
calibration/normalization steps as well as chip-effect normalization
steps involved in the online vignettes.  You can easily skip these,
but for any reasonable analysis I don't see that you should skip the
probe-level summarization step.  In aroma.affymetrix, we refer to the
probe-level summarization as the probe-level modeling (PLM).  Examples
of steps doing that is the RmaCnPlm, AvgCnPlm etc.

The PLMs does not involve normalization.  They only summarize the
probe signals into chip effect estimates.  Maybe your question assumed
that the PLM includes normalization?!?

FYI, in our CRMA paper we compared the impact of different
normalization steps (e.g. Figure 3);

H. Bengtsson; R. Irizarry; B. Carvalho; T.P. Speed, Estimation and
assessment of raw copy numbers at the single locus level,
Bioinformatics, 2008. [pmid: 18204055] [doi:
10.1093/bioinformatics/btn016].

Cheers

Henrik

messages.body_plain:
Hi Marco,

On Tue, Jul 22, 2008 at 3:55 AM, marco <marco...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Dear All,
>
>  I wonder if there is any place where a legend and some explanation of
> the graphical results can be found.

Except from source code (and asking here), that information is
currently not available elsewhere.

>
> 1. There is a \sigma_\Delta on top of the plots, what does this refers
> to and how should this be interpreted? I tried to look in the cited
> paper but I did not find any obvious explanation there.

The \sigma_\Delta is a estimate of the standard deviation of the raw
CNs on that particular chromosome.  The \Delta indicates that a robust
first-order difference estimator has been used, which has the property
of being robust against the existence of CN aberrations.

>
> 2. From my understanding green is the raw and black is the modelled
> results ?

Since I know the source code and you refer to "\sigma_\Delta" above, I
guess that you are running the CbsModel segmentation, correct?  For
the CbsModel, yes, the raw CNs are plotted as green dots and the CN
regions found by CBS are plotted as black lines.

>
> 3. Are the black lines always plotted on top of the green ones, so
> they cannot be hidden by the green ones? I have a lot of black spots
> but seems that they are mostly plotted for relative CN >1 or <-1

The raw CNs are always plotted first.  CN regions are plotted on top
of that.  The "black spots" (should be lines) are probably extremely
short regions identified by CBS.  Have you tried to zoom in?

When you say "CN >1 or <-1", do you mean they are extreme?  It sounds
like you might have quite noisy data.  If so, many of those regions
are likely to be false (positives).  It is hard to say more since you
don't say how many samples you have, what you use as a reference, what
processing steps you've done and so on.

>
> 4. I have run 2 arrays 6.0 and looked at the CNs. The arrays are
> generated from two monozygotic twins, so should be identical up to
> somatic mutations of the tissue used.
> I find some 50-100 tiny small CNs per chromosome but seems like that
> for the most of those the relative CN  is positive. Shouldn't one
> expect that the relative CN is distributed simmetrically around zero ?

Are you doing a paired or non-paired comparison of the two twins?  I
need to know more about your samples and the number of samples you
have to give any decent comments on this.  I wouldn't expect the CN
errors to be perfectly symmetrical.  Remember, we are working on the
log-scale and the tail goes to negative infinity as the underlying CN
goes to zero.  It does not go to positive infinity as the CN increases
(because there is saturation effect and there are no true inifinite
CNs).

Next time, please be more specific what analysis you have done.  That
makes it is easier for anyone to be more specific in their answers.

Cheers

Henrik

>
>
>
> Best Regards
>
> Marco
>
>
> >

cesB <- extract(cesN, c(2,4,8,13))

set, i.e. there is no discussion on non-polymorphic loci (CN probes)
in that paper.  The CN probes were introduced in GWS5 and GWS6.  Both
SNPs & CN probes are processed in the above script.

The "n=..." annotation is the number of *finite* raw CNs on the
chromosome.  Sometimes you get a few NAs and those are not counted.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ana.

You should be able to process 32 samples easily on a Mac with 2Gb.

You have control over the amount of memory used with the 'ram'
argument in the 'fit' method.  By default, it is set to 1.  You could
try setting it to something lower, such as:

fit(plmGene,verbose=verbose,ram=.5)

Basically, all that does is splits the fitting into more chunks, thus
requiring less memory for each chunk.  It will probably only take a
small amount of extra time.

Also, check whether you have objects already loaded in your R session
that may be consuming some space.

Hope that helps.
Mark

This is what I suspected.  When doing probe summarization, a so called
"monocell CDF" is needed.  If missing, it is created automatically
from the main CDF.  This is only done the very first time you use a
CDF never used before.  When it is created, aroma.affymetrix will
always find it.  You run into memory problem while aroma.affymetrix
tries to create this file.

You can create "manually" by doing:

cdf <- cdfEnsb;  # or whatever CDF you are using in the PLM.
cdfM <- getMonocellCdf(cdf, ram=0.5, verbose=verbose);

As you see, this method also takes argument 'ram' so you can create
the monocell CDF on computers with small memory.  If you still have
problems, try a smaller value on 'ram', or redo it in a fresh R
session before any data analysis.  When you can do print(cdfM)
afterwards, you never have to do this again.

FYI, in next release the 'ram' argument to fit() will be passed down
to the internally called getMonocellCdf(), which hopefully will
increase your chances to succeed with Mark's suggestion.

Hope this helps

Henrik

messages.subject: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] Re: ExonRmaPlm - memory error
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I've committed a patch that is more memory efficient.  In your case
you run out of memory while it validates the correctness of the
created file. Apply the patch (only needed once until next release):

library(aroma.affymetrix);
downloadPackagePatch("aroma.affymetrix");

Before you retry, make sure you remove the temporary CDF file:
annotationData/chipTypes/HuEx-1_0-
st-v2/HuEx-1_0-st-v2,U-Ensembl49,G-Affy,monocell.CDF.tmp

Sorry for the mess.  We could send you a pre-created monocell CDF, but
I rather want to identify inefficiencies in aroma.affymetrix so others
can avoid this problem in the future.

Let us know how it goes.

Henrik

Hi,

I just downloaded the HuEx-1_0-st-v2,U-Ensembl49,G-Affy.cdf and tried
the same on my Windows laptop with 1.5GB RAM and my memory peaks at
~180MB, which is not even close to what you get.  Moreover, when I
compare my verbose output to yours it is not the same.  For instance,
you report:

> > cdfM <- getMonocellCdf(cdf, ram=0.1, verbose=verbose)

>  Writes 20000 units...
>    Units left: 19000, 18000, 17000, 16000, 15000, 14000, 13000,
> 12000, 11000, 10000, 9000, 8000, 7000, 6000, 5000, 4000, 3000, 2000,
> 1000, 0, 0
>  Writes 20000 units...done

where as I get:

  Writes 276 units...
    Units left: 0
  Writes 276 units...done

When I use ram=1 (default), I get

  Writes 2768 units...
    Units left: 1768, 768, 0
  Writes 2768 units...done

Does the number of units written in each chunk change when you change
the value of 'ram'?   Even if it doesn't I don't really get why it
tries to write exactly 20,000 units per chunk.

So, now I am starting to wonder if your main CDF is corrupt.  Please
compare the following output with what you get:

Hi

I checked the file size and the checksum and it is different from
yours. Thus, there should have been a problem when I downloaded the
file.
I tried again the ExonRMAPlm (with ram=1) using a new downloaded file
and it runs ok.

I am so sorry for all the work that you had. Next time I will recheck
the files also.

Thank you for eveything
Ana

messages.subject: FIRMA and limma
messages.body_plain:
Hi

First of all, I would like to congratulate you all for the excellent
work that you have done with aroma.affymetrix package and  FIRMA
method.
I am comparing two groups with replicates using Affy Exon arrays.
I read your recent paper describing FIRMA and I want to apply your
method. I have some questions and I would like to know if I am doing
the correct analysis.

After the normalization I did the summarization:
>setCdf(dsQNorm, cdfEnsb)
>plmGene <- ExonRmaPlm(dsQNorm, mergeGroups=TRUE,tag=c("*","ensb"))
>fit(plmGene, verbose=verbose)
>rs<-calculateResiduals(plmGene,verbose=verbose)
>rs<-getResidualSet(plmGene)
>cesGene <- getChipEffectSet(plmGene)

1) To find the genes differentially expressed I extracted the chip
effects (and applied the log2) and proceed to the limma analysis. Just
to confirm, the chipEffects values correspond to expression levels and
the result of limma analysis will be the usual log2 fold-changes?
Do you recommend the filters that you applied in FIRMA paper for
detecting splicing events (minimum probes number and minimum
expression values) also for detecting differentially expressed genes?
How can I obtain the number of probes per PSR?

2) To find the splicing events I did:
>firma <- FirmaModel(plmGene,tag=c("*","ensb"))
>fit(firma,verbose=verbose,force=T)
>fst<-getFirmaScores(firma)
>fstDF<-extractDataFrame(fst,addNames=TRUE)

After this can I apply the same filters as described in 1) and proceed
to limma with fstDF object?
What it will be the fold-change value for a specific exon inclusion/
exclusion event, residuals or FIRMA scores?

Thank you in advance
Ana Grosso

> the result of limma analysis will be the usual log2 fold-changes?

Yes, in fact if you run RMA background correction + quantile
normalization + ExonRmaPlm (mergeGroups=TRUE), you'll get practically
identical values to the defaults from 'fitPLM' in the 'affyPLM'
package.  Therefore, limma on the chip effects from aroma.affymetrix
will be identical to limma on a 'exprs' extraction from a PLMset object.

> Do you recommend the filters that you applied in FIRMA paper for
> detecting splicing events (minimum probes number and minimum
> expression values) also for detecting differentially expressed genes?
> How can I obtain the number of probes per PSR?

If you are using the 'core' set or Ensembl set of probes, I'd say you
shouldn't need to filter out probes for expression analysis.  Most of
the bad behaving probes would be downweighted in the RMA robust model
fit.

Somebody might know a quicker way, but to get the number of probes per
PSR, I would do something like:

# read in data for 1 file (here, i've just read the first 10 units)
x<-readCelUnits(getPathname(getFile(csN,
1)),cdf=getPathname(cdf),units=1:10)

# unwrap the list structure
np<-unlist(lapply(x,FUN=function(uu) { lapply(uu,FUN=function(u)
length(u$intensities)) }))

# to match up to extractDataFrame (again, i've read just 10 units)
exFirma <- extractDataFrame(fs,addNames=TRUE,units=1:10)

exon inclusion/exclusion, but I have done limma analysis on the FIRMA

messages.body_plain:
Mark Robinson wrote:
>

>> Do you recommend the filters that you applied in FIRMA paper for
>> detecting splicing events (minimum probes number and minimum
>> expression values) also for detecting differentially expressed genes?
>> How can I obtain the number of probes per PSR?
>
> If you are using the 'core' set or Ensembl set of probes, I'd say you
> shouldn't need to filter out probes for expression analysis.  Most of
> the bad behaving probes would be downweighted in the RMA robust model
> fit.
>

I would agree that in general, the filtering is not so necessary *for
these reduced set of probes*; more important is probably the number of
probesets (and probes) per gene. I would have a lot of doubt about 1 or
2 probesets being able to find subtle differences because of the level
of noise they would have, but it would just depend on the gene. The main
reason for the filtering for the alternative splicing is that it is very
difficult to tell with only four probes differential splicing events
from differences in non-expressed probesets due solely to background noise.

> Somebody might know a quicker way, but to get the number of probes per
> PSR, I would do something like:
>

There's actually a function in affyxparser package that gets the number
of entries per group (which is the number of probes per probeset for our
cdfs) call readCdfNbrOfCellsPerUnitGroup; it returns it in a list fashion
units<-1:10
x<-readCdfNbrOfCellsPerUnitGroup(getPathname(cdf),unit=units)

If you apply it to the default cdf distributed by Affy, where each
probeset is also a unit (no grouping into genes) then you can get
specific probesets more easily (rather than units/genes). For example,
if you have firma scores under fsDF (and if you chose add.names=TRUE)

mypbsets<-fsDF[1:10,"groupName"] #the first ten probesets, but could do all
affyUnits<-indexOf(cdfAffy,names=mypbsets) #gets their unit number in
the affy cdf, which I've called cdfAffy
nProbesPerExon<-readCdfNbrOfCellsPerUnitGroup(getPathname(cdfAffy),unit=mypbsets)
nProbesPerExonVector<-unlist(nProbesPerExon)

You could do the same thing, I guess, with the ensembl or other cdfs by
first doing
myunits<-unique(fsDF[1:10,"unit"])
allnProbesPerExon<-readCdfNbrOfCellsPerUnitGroup(getPathname(cdfEnsb),unit=myunits),recursive=FALSE)
nProbesPerExon<-unlist(allnProbesPerExon,recursive=FALSE)
nProbesPerExonVector<-unlist(nProbesPerExon)

but I haven't checked that.

I personally am very wary about unlisting complicated lists and matching
things up. I generally worry that I might have the wrong cdf here or
there and things won't match and I won't know. I used unlist above to
get a vector of number of probes, but if you don't you'll realize that
there only a single number per element of the list so it feels
comparatively 'safe' to me. I also like to make everything match up
names as a double check, rather than just the order.

Best,
Elizabeth

messages.subject: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] Re: Custom Canine SNP
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

that error is due to an assertion that test for "too many" missing
values, which would indicate that something went wrong in the earlier
step of the processing.  This is useful when you batch process you
data.

The default threshold is 20% missing values.  You can change this by
specifying argument 'maxNAFraction', e.g.

rawCNs <- extractRawCopyNumbers(cbs, array=1, chromosome=1, maxNAFraction=3/5);

More importantly, you get > 50% missing values while processing your
arrays.  That's quite a bit, especially if you expect Chr1 to be a
copy neutral chromosome.  For humans, you can get quite a few missing
values for females on ChrY because there you have CN=0 and your
estimated signals are close to zero or even non-positive which turn
into NAs on the log-scale.

The allelic crosstalk estimates and corrects for offset and crosstalk.
 This correction introduce non-positive probe signals.  This cause a
problem on the log scale.  To protect against this, we shift probe
signals shift=+300 before doing the summarization.  The summarization
in turn lower the risk for non-positive estimates, but not completely.
 Thus, some non-positive signals will remain and show up as
non-positive chip effect estimates if you use the AvgPlm and NAs if
you use RmaPlm.  For a detailed discussion on this, see the CRMA
paper:

H. Bengtsson; R. Irizarry; B. Carvalho; T.P. Speed, Estimation and
assessment of raw copy numbers at the single locus level,
Bioinformatics, 2008. [pmid: 18204055] [doi:
10.1093/bioinformatics/btn016]

As a first run, you could replace the AllelicCrosstalkCalibration with
a QuantileNormalization.  That will you a "lower bound" on what kind
of raw CN estimates you can get.

Note, don't expect too much with only five arrays (I am working on
methods to improve this, but that's far in the future).  I recommend
you to get more references.  If they are from the same facility that
is even better.   Have Broad check with other group who run
DogSty06m520431 and see if they are (also) willing to share their data
anonymously.  It's a win-win situation for everyone.

Cheers

Henrik

Hi Xuejiang.

The Affy 'unsupported' CDF can be downloaded from:
http://www.affymetrix.com/Auth/support/downloads/library_files/HuGene-1_0-st-v1.r3.unsupported-cdf.zip

I think that is a text version of the CDF.  Before using it within
aroma.affymetrix, you'll want to use 'convertCdf' in the affxparser
package to convert it into the binary version.  You can use it from
the text version, but it is *much* faster with the binary version.

I have also created an experimental Ensembl-centric CDF (just by
remapping the probes) for the Gene 1.0 array, which may be of
interest ... you can download it from:
http://bioinf.wehi.edu.au/folders/mrobinson/exon/human_cdfs/HuGene-1_0-st-v1_Ensembl47.cdf

Hope that gets you started.

Cheers,
Mark

Hi Jay.

I personally haven't worked with the Mouse Exon array yet, but one of
my colleagues at WEHI has.  I believe she used a converted version of
the CDF file from brainarray.

Goto:
http://brainarray.mbni.med.umich.edu/Brainarray/Database/CustomCDF/CDF_download_v10.asp

There are several different versions there.  If you wanted Unigene
identifiers, for example, you could download the zip file from:
http://brainarray.mbni.med.umich.edu/Brainarray/Database/CustomCDF/cdf10/MmEx10stv1_Mm_UG.zip

Again, that is a text version of the CDF.  Use 'convertCdf' to make it
a binary version as aroma.affymetrix will operate much quicker on it.

.... Unfortunately, these CDFs will not allow you to do differential
splicing analysis (e.g. FIRMA).  We'd need to make a correctly
formatted CDF for this.  That should not be difficult to do, just need
an afternoon to sort it out.  Let me know if you'll be needing this
and I'll put it on my TO DO list.

Mark

messages.body_plain:
Hi Mark,

I just want to check wheather several mouse genes are expressied in
exon level (full).
so I download CEL files from affymetrix web page to get probesets'
values in different tissues.
http://www.affymetrix.com/support/technical/sample_data/exon_array_data.affx
I also download CDF file from WEHI as below.
http://bioinf.wehi.edu.au/folders/ken/exon/MoEx-1_0-st-v1.cdf.

when I executed my souce code

cdf <- AffymetrixCdfFile$fromChipType("MoEx-1_0-st-v1")
cs <- AffymetrixCelSet$fromName("TP_M_full", cdf=cdf)
bc <- RmaBackgroundCorrection(cs)
csBC <- process(bc,verbose=verbose)

csBC

qn <- QuantileNormalization(csBC, typesToUpdate="pm")

print(qn)

csN <- process(qn, verbose=verbose)
plm <- ExonRmaPlm(csN, mergeGroups=FALSE)
fit(plm, verbose=verbose)
chp<-getChipEffectSet(plm)
cdf_1 <- getCdf(chp)
theta <- extractMatrix(chp, returnUgcMap=TRUE);

ugcMap <- attr(theta, "unitGroupCellMap");
un<-getUnitNames(cdf_1, ugcMap[,"unit"]);
rownames(theta) <- un
write.table(log2(theta), file = "full.mouse.csv")

I got a matrix in file "full.mouse.csv":

                "moex_wta_brain_A" "moex_wta_brain_B"......
"4304920" 4.75438649978744 5.05010056444324 ......
"4304920" 5.64492522300038 5.23884115844359 .....
"4304920" 5.87239382792488 5.96080976185133 .....
"4304920" 5.4875023679347 5.52650676111341 .....
"4304921" 4.69653386918019 3.4518337787065 .....
"4304921" 4.50483971346476 4.96101076516952 .....
"4304921" 2.68863695269967 2.30223184674608 .....
......

each row should corresponds to one probeset. but in this matrix,
the same probeset id appears in mutiple rows.

moeover, I did:

> chp<-getChipEffectSet(plm)
> theta <- extractMatrix(chp, returnUgcMap=TRUE);
> un<-getUnitNames(cdf, ugcMap[,"unit"]);
> un[1:20]
 [1] "4304920" "4304920" "4304920" "4304920" "4304921" "4304921"
"4304921"
 [8] "4304921" "4304921" "4304921" "4304921" "4304921" "4304921"
"4304921"
[15] "4304921" "4304921" "4304921" "4304921" "4304921" "4304922"
> gp<-getUnitNames(cdf, ugcMap[,"group"]);
> gp[1:20]
 [1] "4304920" "4304921" "4304922" "4304923" "4304920" "4304921"
"4304922"
 [8] "4304923" "4304925" "4304927" "4304928" "4304929" "4304930"
"4304931"
[15] "4304932" "4304933" "4304934" "4304935" "4304937" "4304920"
> cl<-getUnitNames(cdf, ugcMap[,"cell"]);
> cl[1:20]
 [1] "4304920" "4304921" "4304922" "4304923" "4304925" "4304927"
"4304928"
 [8] "4304929" "4304930" "4304931" "4304932" "4304933" "4304934"
"4304935"
[15] "4304937" "4304938" "4304939" "4304940" "4304941" "4304942"

I doubt the CDF is not correct as said in the beginning of this
thread.
Now I am trying to find out the probeset id for each row of the
matrix.
if you have any ideas, please give advices.

J.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Mark,

Thank you very much for your kind information. But I still got stuck
with the Cdf annotation problem.

I downloaded the cdf file from
http://www.affymetrix.com/Auth/support/downloads/library_files/HuGene-1_0-st-v1.r3.unsupported-cdf.zip

And according to the instruction I converted the ASCII file to binary
using "convertCdf". The converted Cdf file works fine for
"AffymetrixCelSet$fromName". And "getCdf" can return correct Cdf
settings. However, I cannot use the Cdf file correctly because I
usually get warning message of "could not find a CDF file for this

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

The reason aroma.affymetrix is complaining is because the CEL header
says that the chip is of type HuGene-1_0-st-v1, but the CDF file has a
different name (HuGene-1_0-st-v1.r3.cdf).  Also, your directory
structure does not conform to that expected by the package.  Please
see the page at

http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/setup

Could you please try the following steps and let us know if you still
experience a problem:

- create a subdirectory HuGene-1_0-st-v1 in annotationData/chipTypes/
- rename your CDF to
annotationData/chipTypes/HuGene-1_0-st-v1/HuGene-1_0-st-v1,r3.cdf
(note the comma in the file name, not a period)
- when you set up the cdf, do: cdf <-
AffymetrixCdfFile$fromChipType("HuGene-1_0-st-v1", tags="r3")

Cheers,

Ken

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

If I understand you correctly, it looks like you are asking how to get
the segmentation results for all arrays and all chromosomes (correct
me if I'm wrong) and also to display the results, rather than fitting
separately.  To do this just use the following code:

ce <- ChromosomeExplorer(cbs)
process(ce, arrays=1:7, chromosomes=1:23, verbose=verbose)
display(ce)

Note that this may take some time, so be prepared to wait.

I think I see where you have got confused with the vignette - we'll
update to make it a bit clearer.

Cheers

Ken

On Sat, Jul 26, 2008 at 3:06 AM, yupu <yupu...@gmail.com> wrote:

[snip]

> So here are my questions:
> 1-- I think the raw copy number is alreay in log scale, right?
> 2-- what would I need to do to map x to the snp_id? -- as i remember
> there was some utility method from bioconductor that do similar
> mapping for affymetrix's expression data set. Do we have these for the
> snp data?
> 3-- These are the CN for each probe, not the probe set, right?

1. Yes.
2. You will have to go back to the annotation files provided by
Affymetrix.  There is a CSV file available from the netaffx website
for each SNP chip and this contains information such as SNP IDs.
There was a discussion on this issue a few days ago (try searching the
group archive).
3. No, they are for the probe set (unit).  See the discussion on
"Extract raw copy number using Aroma" from last week.

Cheers,

Ken
